parole.significato: head
parole.testo: From French -céphalie, German -zephalie, or Latin -cephalia, from Ancient Greek κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) and a suffix: French -ie, German -ie, or Latin -ia.

parole.significato: describes something which is formed in a certain way or produces something
parole.testo: From French -gène and German -gen, from Latin -genus and Ancient Greek -γενής (-genḗs).

parole.significato: A white crystalline resinous substance extracted from gutta-percha by the action of alcohol or ether.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French albane (in the form alban, respelt after the German Alban), from the Latin albus (“white”) + the French -ane (“-an”).

parole.significato: The view that all knowledge is derived from sense experience; empiricism as opposed to apriorism.
parole.testo: From French apostériorisme or German Aposteriorismus, ultimately from Latin ā posteriōrī (“from what follows”). By surface analysis, a posteriori + -ism.

parole.significato: A kind of clown, usually serving as an anarchic foil to the whiteface.
parole.testo: From French auguste, from German (dumme) August.

parole.significato: A heterocyclic compound derived from pyrimidine that is the basis of all barbiturate drugs.
parole.testo: Mid 19th century from French barbiturique, from German Barbitursäure, from Barbara + Säure (“acid”), related to Latin urea.

parole.significato: An alkaloid, C₈H₁₀N₄O₂, found naturally in tea and coffee plants, which acts as a mild stimulant on the central nervous…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French caféine, from café (“coffee”), or German Caffein, Kaffein (cp. Coffein, Koffein), from Kaffee (“coffee”) (cp. Kaffe, Koffee, Koffe), or Italian caffè (“coffee”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A ceramic raw material with a high percentage of silica and alumina.
parole.testo: From French chamotte, from German Schamotte, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: A chaplet of rue, as used as a charge on the arms of Saxony.
parole.testo: From French crancelin, from German Kränzlein (“small garland”).

parole.significato: A type of organ reed stop, sounding a tone resembling that of the oboe.
parole.testo: From French cromorne, from German Krummhorn (“crooked horn, cornet, an organ pipe turned like a trumpet”). Doublet of krummhorn.

parole.significato: Either of two species, Desmana moschata or Galemys pyrenaicus, of aquatic or semiaquatic insectivore of the mole family…
parole.testo: From French desman, German Desman, from Swedish desmanråtta (“muskrat”), from desman (“musk”, older also desma, desme), from Middle Low German dēsem, from Old Saxon desamo, alteration of *besamo (cf. Old High German bisamo), from Late Latin bisamum (“musk”), from Hebrew בושם (bāśām, bōśem). Doublet

parole.significato: Someone who writes or adapts theater plays; a playwright or dramatist, especially one connected with a specific theater…
parole.testo: * Definition 1: Borrowed from French dramaturge. * Definition 2: Borrowed from German Dramaturg.

parole.significato: A rock surface with a crust of tiny crystals.
parole.testo: Borrowed via French from German Druse (“crystallized piece of ore”); compare dross.

parole.significato: A learning disability characterized by reading and writing difficulties.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French dyslexie and/or German Dyslexie, coined by German ophthalmologist Rudolf Berlin in 1887, from dys- + lexis + -ia, from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-) + λέξις (léxis, “diction”, “word”), from Ancient Greek λέγω (légō, “to speak”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leg- (“t

parole.significato: The layout of a publication or document.
parole.testo: Via French format and German Format, from New Latin liber fōrmātus (“book fashioned”), from fōrmō (“to shape, fashion”).

parole.significato: A mainly French and Flemish type of tapestry having richly coloured pictorial designs.
parole.testo: Named after a Parisian manufacturing company founded by Jean Gobelin, whose French name derives from German Kobold (“evil gnome”).

parole.significato: A clear brandy made from black cherries: kirschwasser.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French kirsch, from German Kirschwasser (“cherry water”). Doublet of cerise and cherry.

parole.significato: A fermented drink made from mare's milk, common among peoples of the Central Asian steppes.
parole.testo: Via French koumis, German Kumiss, from Russian кумы́с (kumýs), borrowed from a Turkic source. Compare Tatar кымыз (qımız), Kazakh қымыз (qımız), Kyrgyz кымыз (kımız), Southern Altai кымыс (kïmïs), Turkish kımız, Azerbaijani qımız, Northern Altai кымыс (kïmïs), etc.

parole.significato: Any of a class of German mercenaries of the 15th and 16th centuries, most of whom were pikemen and foot soldiers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lansquenet, from German Landsknecht, from Lands (“of the land”) + Knecht (“servant”). Doublet of Landsknecht.

parole.significato: To make (a state or leader under the Holy Roman Empire) into a mediate vassal rather than an immediate one, directly un…
parole.testo: From French médiatiser, German mediatisieren.

parole.significato: A type of reed organ, similar to a harmonium.
parole.testo: Alternative form of melodeon. Both this word and its variant melodeon are ultimately borrowings from French French mélodium and German German Melodium. Attested from 1846.

parole.significato: Any of the pathways on the body along which chi or qi (life force) is thought to flow and, therefore, the acupoints are…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French méridien or German Meridian (“pathway on the body along which life force is thought to flow”), from Latin merīdiānum (“midday; position of the sun at noon; the south”) (see further at etymology 2); the French and German words are calques of Mandarin 經 /经, 经 (jīng, “pathway on th

parole.significato: Willingness of action especially in behavior.
parole.testo: From motive (verb) + -ation, probably after French motivation and German Motivation.

parole.significato: Synonym of nonpareil.
parole.testo: (printing): From French nonpareille and German Nonpareille (“6-point type”).

parole.significato: Relating to paratonia.
parole.testo: From para- + tonic. In specific use in the medical sense, after French paratonique. In the botanical sense, after German paratonisch.

parole.significato: A native or resident of Georgia in the United States.
parole.testo: * As an English surname, from French péché (“sin”). Compare Peachey, Petch. * As a German surname, Americanized from Pietsch.

parole.significato: A general belief that bad things will happen.
parole.testo: From French pessimisme, from Latin pessimus (“worst”) + -ism, superlative of malus (“bad”). As a doctrine, from German Pessimismus as used by the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer in 1819.

parole.significato: Synonym of brevier.
parole.testo: From French petit (“brevier”) directly or via German Petit (“brevier”).

parole.significato: Someone who solicits customers for prostitution and acts as manager for a group of prostitutes; a pander.
parole.testo: Origin unknown. Perhaps from French pimpant (“smart, sparkish”) or German Pimpf (“a boy, a youth, a young squirt”). The Old English near-synonym was rendered by Old English forspennend (literally “a solicitor”).

parole.significato: A lively dance originating in Bohemia.
parole.testo: Via French and German from Czech polka, variant of půlka (“half”) as in "half-step"; see půl (“half”).

parole.significato: An aliphatic hydrocarbon, C₃H₈, a constituent of natural gas.
parole.testo: From clipping of propionic acid + -ane, from French propionique, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró) + πίων (píōn, “fat”). Analyzable as prop- + -ane, borrowing or calque of German Propan.

parole.significato: Any of numerous large, complex naturally-produced molecules composed of one or more long chains of amino acids, in whic…
parole.testo: From proto- + -ein. Suggested by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in a letter to Gerardus Johannes Mulder, from French protéine and German Protein, both coined based on Ancient Greek πρωτεῖος (prōteîos, “primary”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”).

parole.significato: A light dumpling made of lightly spiced minced meat or fish bound with egg and poached.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French quenelle, from German Knödel. Doublet of knaidel.

parole.significato: A dark-skinned variety of plum.
parole.testo: From French quetsche, from Lorraine German Quetsche (standard German Zwetschge), ultimately from Latin damascēna. Doublet of damson.

parole.significato: The sand leek, Allium scorodoprasum
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rocambole, from regional German Rockenbolle.

parole.significato: A lozenge with a smaller round hole in the centre, showing the field (rarely used).
parole.testo: From French rustre, from German Raute.

parole.significato: A light sword with a curved blade, sharp along the front edge, part of the back edge, and at the point.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sabre, from German Säbel, from Polish szabla, from Hungarian szablya. Cognate with Danish sabel, Russian са́бля (sáblja), Serbo-Croatian сабља, Sicilian sciàbbula.

parole.significato: A leather pocket or pouch worn hanging from a cavalry officer’s belt.
parole.testo: From French sabretache, from German Säbeltasche, from Säbel (“sabre”) and Tasche (“pocket”).

parole.significato: A leather case or pocket worn by cavalry at the left side, suspended from the swordbelt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sabretache, from German.

parole.significato: The enjoyment of inflicting pain or humiliation without pity.
parole.testo: From French sadisme and German Sadismus. Named after the Marquis de Sade, famed for his libertine writings depicting the pleasure of inflicting pain to others. The word for "sadism" (sadisme) was coined or acknowledged in the 1834 posthumous reprint of French lexicographer Boiste's Dictionnaire univ

parole.significato: zander, pikeperch (fish)
parole.testo: From French sandre, from German Zander. Doublet of zander.

parole.significato: A light blue color, with a tint of grey.
parole.testo: From French Saxe (“Saxony”) (from German), where a dye of this color originated.

parole.significato: A short-term standing wave oscillation of the water level in a lake, or other confined body of water such as a fjord, c…
parole.testo: From Swiss French seiche, perhaps from German Seiche (“sinking”).

parole.significato: Person who experiments carelessly, without paying attention to the possible consequences of their experiments and witho…
parole.testo: Calque of French apprenti-sorcier, itself a calque of German Zauberlehrling.

parole.significato: A vehicle that may be hired for single journeys by members of the public, particularly one with an automated meter to c…
parole.testo: Shortened from taximeter cab, taximeter (“automatic meter that records distance and fare”) from French taximètre, from German Taxameter (whence also English taxameter), coined from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”). More at tax, task. The aviation sense originally derived from a slang term for tra

parole.significato: A device installed in a taxicab that calculates the fare based upon distance travelled and waiting time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French taximètre, from German Taxameter, coined from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”), from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g- (“to touch, handle”).

parole.significato: The study of the design or final purpose of natural occurrences, that is, of such occurrences being the result of inten…
parole.testo: Partly borrowed from French téléologie and from German Teleologie + English -logy (suffix denoting a branch of learning or study of a particular subject). Téléologie and Teleologie are both derived from Late Latin teleologia, from Ancient Greek τέλεος (téleos) (the genitive singular of τέλος (télos,

parole.significato: A treatise on terms, especially those used in a specialised field.
parole.testo: From French terminologie or German Terminologie and their source, New Latin terminologia, from Medieval Latin terminus (“a term”) + -ologia (“study of”), from -o- (“(interconsonantal)”) + -logia, from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “-logy, branch of study, to speak”).

parole.significato: Embalming.
parole.testo: From French thanatopraxie, German Thanatopraxie, Spanish tanatopraxia, ultimately from Ancient Greek θάνατος (thánatos, “dead body”) + πρᾶξις (prâxis, “practice”). Doublet of thanatopraxis.

parole.significato: A large brass musical instrument, usually in the bass range, played through a vibration of the lips upon the mouthpiece…
parole.testo: Borrowed in the 19th century from French tuba (“tuba”), German Tuba (“tuba”), originally Baß-Tuba (literally “bass tuba”), or Italian tuba (“tuba”), from Latin tuba (“tube, trumpet, military trumpet”). The Latin term is of obscure ultimate origin, but is possibly connected to tībia (“shinbone, reed-

parole.significato: A lancer, a soldier armed with a lance in a former light cavalry unit of the Polish, Prussian or German, Austrian, and…
parole.testo: From French uhlan, from German Uhlan, from Polish ułan, from Ottoman Turkish اوغلان (oğlan).

parole.significato: A mythological creature (usually humanoid and undead) said to feed on the blood or life energy of the living.
parole.testo: From French vampire, from German Vampir, via Hungarian from a Slavic word, probably Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr /ва̀мпӣр, from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь, further possibly from Proto-Turkic *ōpur (“glutton, witch, evil spirit”), or from native construction. Doublet of dhampir and oupire.

parole.significato: A dry, or sweet apéritif wine flavored with aromatic herbs, and often used in mixed drinks.
parole.testo: From French vermout, vermouth, from German Wermut (“wormwood”). Doublet of wormwood.

parole.significato: A large, round, semi-permanent tent with vertical walls and a conical roof, usually associated with Central Asia and Mo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French yourte or German Jurte, from Russian ю́рта (júrta, “yurt”), from a Turkic language, from Proto-Turkic *yūrt (“dwelling place”).
